etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English breden, from Old English brēdan, from Proto-Germanic *brōdijaną (“to brood”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“warm”). Cognate with Scots brede, breid, Saterland Frisian briede, West Frisian briede, Dutch broeden, German Low German bröden, German brüten.

definitions.definition: To produce offspring sexually; to bear young.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, David Van Tassel, Lee DeHaan, “Wild Plants to the Rescue”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3:
quote.text: Plant breeding is always a numbers game. […] The wild species we use are rich in genetic variation, and individual plants are highly heterozygous and do not breed true. In addition, we are looking for rare alleles, so the more plants we try, the better.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give birth to; to be the native place of.

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: Yet every mother breeds not sons alike.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To keep (animals) and have (them) reproduce in a way that improves the next generation's qualities.
(transitive, often with to or with) To arrange the mating of (specific animals).
To propagate or grow (plants) in an effort to give (them) certain qualities.
To take care of in infancy and through childhood; to bring up.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To be formed in the parent or dam; to be generated or to grow, like young before birth.
(sometimes as breed up) To educate; to instruct; to bring up.

definitions.definition: To produce or obtain by any natural process.
